opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest value is scale and diversity. With a traditional physics simulator, every scene has to be built by hand. Someone models the objects, sets up the materials, the lighting, the textures, and tunes the physics parameters. That's very expensive, so in practice you end up with a fairly limited set of environments. And no matter how much effort you put in, there's always a gap between what the simulator renders and what the real world looks like. That's the sim-to-real gap we've been fighting in robotics for years.

Video generation models are trained on enormous amounts of real-world video, so they've absorbed a huge amount of knowledge about how the world looks and, to some extent, how it behaves. With just a text prompt or an image you can create a kitchen, a warehouse, a messy living room, an outdoor street, in endless variations. That long tail of diversity is exactly what robot learning needs, because a robot deployed in the real world will run into situations nobody thought to model.

The other point is realism. Generated videos can look much closer to real camera footage than a typical rendered simulation, so the visual gap shrinks a lot.

But I want to be honest about the limitations. Traditional simulators have something video models don't yet have reliably: physical accuracy and consistency. In a physics engine, if you push a cup, it obeys the equations of motion. Contact, friction, and object permanence are guaranteed. Video models sometimes hallucinate. Objects can deform strangely, appear or disappear, or move in ways that aren't physically plausible. For tasks with a lot of contact-rich manipulation, that matters a lot.

So I don't see it as one replacing the other, at least not yet. I see them as complementary. Simulation gives you precise physics and ground truth, while video generation, or more broadly world models, gives you visual richness, diversity, and common-sense knowledge about the world. Increasingly, I think the direction is toward learned world models that are action-conditioned. You give the model the robot's action, it predicts what happens next, and you can use that for training, for evaluating policies, or even for planning. If these models keep improving in physical consistency, they could become a kind of universal simulator, one you don't have to hand-engineer, which would be a big unlock for scaling robot learning.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts manually building traditional simulation scenes with creating varied scenes from a text prompt.

fable-5.1.text:
Jie Tan: That's a question I think about a lot, because for most of my career the answer was obviously simulation. Simulation gives you physics you can trust, you can run it millions of times in parallel, and it's cheap. That's how we trained our quadruped locomotion policies, and it worked.

But simulation has a ceiling, and the ceiling is content. Someone has to build the world. Someone has to model every object, every material, every texture, every room. If I want a robot to learn to open a thousand different kitchen cabinets, I need someone to make a thousand kitchen cabinets, and realistically nobody does. So you end up with a few dozen hand-crafted environments, and the robot learns those very well and then struggles the moment it sees something slightly different. The sim-to-real gap people talk about is partly a physics gap, but honestly a bigger part is a diversity gap.

Video generation attacks exactly that problem. These models have seen essentially all of human visual experience. They know what kitchens look like, what happens when a cup tips over, how a door swings, how light falls in a cluttered garage. You don't have to author any of that. You give it a starting frame and an action or an instruction, and it produces a plausible continuation. In a sense, the model has compressed an enormous amount of common-sense knowledge about how the world looks and behaves, and we get to borrow it for free.

So the value I see has a few layers. The first is coverage. You can generate scenes and situations that nobody would ever bother to build in a simulator, long-tail stuff. The second is appearance. These videos look real, so the visual domain gap that we used to fight with randomization and domain adaptation largely goes away. And the third, which I think is the most interesting, is that a video model can act as a world model. If you can condition it on the robot's actions, you can roll out imagined futures, evaluate a policy, even do planning, all without touching the real robot.

Now I want to be careful, because I don't think video generation replaces simulation. The physics in these models is approximate. Objects sometimes pass through each other, hands grow extra fingers, contact dynamics are not reliable. For locomotion or anything where precise contact matters, I would still trust a physics engine over a diffusion model. And for the robot's own body you want exact kinematics, not a hallucination.

So the way I think about it is as a hybrid. The simulator gives you the rigorous, verifiable core, especially for dynamics and contacts. The video model gives you the world around the robot, the visual richness and the diversity. Over time I expect the video models to become more physically consistent, and I expect simulators to become more generative, and the two will meet somewhere in the middle. But today, the real value of video generation is that it finally lets us scale the content side of simulation, which has been the bottleneck for years.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts manually building many scenes with video generation and says it can be given an instruction, but it does not clearly identify varying language prompts as the alternative.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest value is the diversity of scenes you could create. In traditional simulation, you have to build the environment: the geometry, the objects, the textures, and how things move. That gives you a lot of control, but creating a large variety of realistic environments takes substantial effort.

With video generation, you could describe a scene and generate variations—different lighting, different objects, different situations. For robotics, that could help expose a model to situations that would be expensive to construct individually in a simulator.

The challenge is that a video can look realistic without being physically correct. And a robot needs more than a video: it needs the environment to respond consistently to its actions. So I see video generation as a promising complement to traditional simulation. It could provide visual richness and diversity, while simulation provides the physical structure and control needed to test behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says traditional simulation requires manually building scene details, while video generation can describe a scene and generate variations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest value is the diversity of scenes you can create. In traditional simulation, you have to build the environment, create the assets, and specify how things behave. That gives you control, but it takes a lot of work, especially if you want to capture the complexity of the real world.

With video generation, you can describe a scene and potentially generate many variations—different lighting, different objects, different environments. For robotics, that could be useful for exposing a model to situations that would be expensive to build individually in a simulator.

The challenge is that a visually convincing video is not necessarily physically correct. And a robot needs more than a video: it needs to take an action and see how the world responds. So I see video generation as a promising complement to traditional simulation, particularly for visual diversity, while physical consistency and interaction remain important problems to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says a scene can be described to generate variations and contrasts this with the work of building scenes in simulation. It does not clearly identify varying language prompts as the alternative.
